analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to buy FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada and other wealthy countries at lower prices.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 110 cosponsors from both parties but was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and two of its subcommittees, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal drug law to let registered pharmacies, wholesalers, and individual consumers import prescription drugs from Canada, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, and the European Union — countries where the same drugs often sell for far less. It would bar drug makers from raising prices for, cutting supply to, or otherwise retaliating against exporters and importers, and it would let consumers buy from vetted foreign pharmacies by mail. The House committee where it landed never brought it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially people on fixed incomes paying cash or with high cost-sharing. The bill's own findings cite CBO research that the same prescription drugs cost 35 to 55 percent less in other developed countries, and that Americans spend over $200 billion a year on prescriptions [S3]. Registered importers — pharmacies, groups of pharmacies, and wholesalers — would gain a new legal business channel, as would licensed foreign pharmacies that sell to individual Americans [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Waives the current ban on importing prescription drugs, allowing commercial importers and individuals (up to a 90-day supply with a valid prescription) to buy qualifying drugs from registered exporters in Canada, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, and the EU [S2][S3].

Prohibits manufacturers from discriminating against importers — charging them higher prices, cutting off or delaying their supplies, refusing to do business with them, or making the drug sold abroad different from the drug sold in the U.S. to frustrate importation; violations are enforced by the FTC as unfair practices [S2][S3].
Declares that reselling in the U.S. a drug properly sold abroad is not patent infringement, removing a legal tool manufacturers could use to block importers [S2].
Requires the FDA to publish a public list of registered exporters and educate consumers, and bars unregistered foreign pharmacies from payment systems, steering buyers toward vetted sellers [S2][S3].

Keeps safety guardrails: importers and exporters must register with the FDA, submit to inspections at least 12 times a year, verify chain of custody from the manufacturer, post bonds, and comply with labeling, packaging, and recall requirements [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose U.S. prices would face competition from lower-priced identical drugs sold abroad, and whose ability to price-discriminate or restrict supply would be curtailed. The program's cost is funded by fees on importers and exporters, capped at 2.5 percent of the price of imported drugs, which would partly flow into import prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: Safety risk: the bill creates a new supply channel for drugs manufactured for foreign markets, and while it requires FDA-approved labeling, chain-of-custody verification, and inspections, critics of importation argue that foreign distribution chains are harder to police and raise the risk of counterfeit or substandard drugs reaching patients [S2][S3].

The bill excludes biologic products, injected and infused drugs, controlled substances, and certain accelerated-approval drugs — so some of the most expensive therapies (monoclonal antibodies, injectable biologics) get no price relief [S3].
Fees on importers and exporters, capped at 2.5 percent of the imported drugs' value plus $10,000 registration fees, add a small cost on top of foreign prices [S3].

Drug makers have argued that importation without addressing foreign price controls mainly imports other countries' price-setting, and that manufacturers might restrict foreign supplies in response; the bill tries to prevent that with anti-discrimination rules, but the arms race between the two is untested [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and favorable for consumers: the same FDA-approved molecules routinely sell for far less abroad, and the bill builds a heavily regulated, registered-importer system rather than opening the borders indiscriminately. The design is intricate — registration, bonds, inspections, fee caps, notice requirements — which raises compliance costs for importers and leaves the FDA with substantial administrative burden, but those costs are modest compared with the potential price gap. The biggest honest caveats are that biologics are left out and that manufacturers would likely fight the anti-discrimination provisions hard, making the achievable savings uncertain in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which passed it along to its Health and its Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection subcommittees, where it sat; neither the committee nor the House ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 10, 2007, by Rep. Rahm Emanuel with an initial bipartisan group of cosponsors, and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5].
On February 2, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection; that is the last action recorded [S5].
It accumulated 109 cosponsors — 93 Democrats and 16 Republicans — but no committee mark-up or floor vote ever occurred during the 110th Congress [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept the U.S. market free of lower-priced foreign competition, and the committee system that let the bill end without a vote.

for.name: Rahm Emanuel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized an initial bipartisan list of 50 founding cosponsors from both parties [S3].

for.name: 16 of 110 cosponsoring House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members like Jo Ann Emerson, Mike Simpson, and Jim Ramstad [S4].

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral, sent it to two subcommittees on February 2, 2007, and never held a mark-up or reported it to the floor [S5].

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturer industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed drug importation legislation, arguing it posed safety risks and undermined prices that fund research; the industry has consistently lobbied against such bills.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was strongly bipartisan — 93 Democrats and 16 Republicans signed on — yet the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral in the House [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill opens the U.S. market to identical drugs sold more cheaply in Canada, Europe, Japan, and elsewhere, and bans price discrimination, supply cutoffs, and product differences aimed at importers. Their loss would come directly out of the price gap American patients currently pay [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Internet and mail-order pharmacies and drug importers
industries.note: The bill creates a legal, regulated channel for registered pharmacies, wholesalers, and exporters to sell lower-priced drugs to Americans, with the FDA publishing a list of vetted exporters. Unregistered foreign pharmacies are barred from payment systems, pushing the market toward registered players [S2][S3].

Registered importers gain the right to buy qualifying drugs abroad and resell them in the U.S., a new profit channel. They bear registration fees, inspection costs capped at 2.5 percent of import value, and compliance obligations in exchange [S3].

The bill expressly leaves in place manufacturers' rebate and formulary discount deals with insurers and PBMs, so their negotiated discounts lose some of their value once patients can comparison-shop across borders; PBMs' arbitrage role between list and net prices would face new competitive pressure [S3].
